extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (also patent applicants and practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and formulating rejections under 35 U.S.C. §101 (subject matter eligibility) including Step 1, Step 2A (Prong One and Two), and Step 2B of the Alice/Mayo framework, and use of streamlined analysis (Pathway A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity / insignificant application
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations that add only insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering in conjunction with a law of nature or abstract idea) do not meaningfully limit a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some cases have identified insignificant computer implementation as an example of insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., Fort Props.; Bancorp Servs.). Examples cited: cutting hair after first determining the hair style (In re Brown); printing or downloading generated menus (Ameranth). For claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity, examiners should explain in an eligibility rejection why they do not meaningfully limit the claim (for example, storing data added to a process that only recites computing a mathematical relationship does not add a meaningful limitation). See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of use / technological environment limitation is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that merely indicate a field of use or technological environment in which to apply a judicial exception do not amount to significantly more than the exception itself and cannot integrate a judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent (e.g., Flook, Bilski, Affinity Labs) show that merely limiting an abstract idea to a particular technological use or device is 'token' and not an inventive concept. Contrast with Diehr, where specific limitations acted in concert to transform a product. Examiners should treat 'technological environment' and 'field of use' interchangeably for eligibility analysis and consider overlap with insignificant extra-solution activity (MPEP § 2106.05(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of field-of-use/technological-environment limitations that are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Court-cited examples of limitations that merely confine an abstract idea to a particular environment or audience and thus fail to make the claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (i–x) include: (i) administering 6-thioguanine to a particular patient population (Mayo); (ii) identifying participants as commodity providers/consumers (Bilski); (iii) limiting C = 2πr to wheels (Flook); (iv) specifying monitoring audit log data occurs in a computer environment (FairWarning); (v) virus screening used within a telephone network or the Internet (Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec); (vi) limiting collecting/analyzing/displaying information to power-grid data (Electric Power Group v. Alstom); (vii) informing doctors to apply a law of nature for genetic polymorphism detection (Genetic Techs. v. Merial); (viii) budgeting implemented using broad communication medium (Internet/telephone) (Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One); (ix) advertising-as-currency used on the Internet (Ultramercial v. Hulu); (x) requiring computer/network/online transaction limitations for guaranteeing performance (buySAFE v. Google). Examiners should explain why such limitations do not meaningfully limit the claim when asserting ineligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis (Pathway A) for self-evident eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: For efficiency, examiners may use a streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident (e.g., the claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The streamlined analysis yields the same result as the full Alice/Mayo test; it is not a way to avoid an ineligibility finding. If there is doubt whether applicant seeks coverage of a judicial exception, the full analysis should be conducted. The record may simply reflect eligibility by absence of a rejection or clarifying remarks. See flowchart in MPEP § 2106, subsection III.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility is self-evident — examples and bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be self-evidently eligible if, when viewed as a whole, it clearly does not seek to tie up any judicial exception (e.g., clearly improves technology or is a complex manufactured industrial product).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a robotic arm assembly with a control system that uses mathematical relationships but does not tie up the math; a nature-based product claim that does not attempt to tie up the nature-based product (artificial hip prosthesis coated with a naturally occurring mineral); claimed products including only ancillary nature-based components (cellphone with gold contact). Claims that are a 'close call' should undergo the full eligibility analysis (see BASCOM example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear improvement to technology or computer functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are directed to clear improvements in computer-related technology or other technological processes may be not abstract and thus may avoid the full eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit examples: Enfish (self-referential table for database — eligible at Step 1), McRO (automatic lip synchronization and facial animation — eligible at Step 1). If claims clearly improve technology/computer functionality, they may qualify for Pathway A or be found not directed to an abstract idea at Step 2A. If unclear ('close call'), perform the full Alice/Mayo analysis (see BASCOM and related discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections must be based on substantive law and review the record as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility rejections must be based on the substantive law under 35 U.S.C. §101 as interpreted by judicial precedent; examiners should review the record as a whole before concluding ineligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examination guidance, training, and examples explain the law but are not themselves a basis for rejection. Examiners should consider the specification, claims, prosecution history, relevant case law, and prior art. Eligibility determinations are claim-by-claim; dependent claims may differ from independent claims. See MPEP §§ 2106.03–2106.06 for substantive law discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie case requirement for eligibility rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: When more likely than not that a claim fails eligibility criteria (Step 1 NO and/or Step 2B NO), examiners should formulate a rejection that sets forth a prima facie case of ineligibility under the substantive law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The initial burden is on the examiner to explain clearly and specifically why a claim is ineligible so the applicant has sufficient notice to respond. The rejection must provide a reasoned explanation that supports the examiner's conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — identify the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject matter eligibility rejection should point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recite the judicial exception and explain why those limitations set forth or describe a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the claim describes but does not expressly set forth the judicial exception, the rejection must explain what subject matter those limitations describe and why that described subject matter is a judicial exception. When the examiner determines a claim recites an abstract idea, the rejection should identify the abstract idea as recited in the claim and explain why it falls within one of the groupings of abstract ideas (mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity) per MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2). See MPEP § 2106.04 for more on Step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — identify additional elements and evaluate integration
rubrics_metrics.description: For Prong Two, the rejection should identify any additional elements beyond the judicial exception and evaluate whether those elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must specifically point to claim features/limitations/steps beyond the identified judicial exception and evaluate the integration using considerations set forth in MPEP §§ 2106.04(d), 2106.05(a)-(c) and (e)-(h). Examiners should give weight to all claimed additional elements in Prong Two, even if those elements represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — explain lack of inventive concept (significantly more)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Step 2B, the rejection should explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim as a whole amounting to significantly more than the identified judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner concludes that certain claim elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activities in the field, the examiner must expressly support the rejection in writing with one of the four options specified in Subsection III. See MPEP § 2106.05 et seq. for guidance on searching for an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point to specific claim limitations when making a rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a subject matter eligibility rejection, the Office action must point to specific claim limitation(s) that recite the judicial exception and explain why each claim is unpatentable with sufficient clarity and specificity to enable applicant to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After establishing the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim, evaluate eligibility of each claim as a whole using MPEP § 2106. The rejection must be sufficiently clear and specific to provide applicant notice and enable effective response. See MPEP § 2111 for claim interpretation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution — state all non-cumulative rejections in first action
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the principles of compact prosecution, examiners should make a complete examination for each claim under all patentability requirements and state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regardless of whether a §101 rejection is made, a complete examination should be made for every claim under §§ 102, 103, 112, and utility/inventorship/double patenting concerns, and non-statutory double patenting. Examiners should include all non-cumulative grounds in the first action.
